newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian premier warns of tough winter ahead.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian premier warns of tough winter ahead.

text.p: Bulgarian Prime Minister Ivan Kostov warned on Sunday the country faced another tough winter as the government carried out IMF-prescribed economic reforms.
He said his government would move quickly with major privatisations and infrastructure projects to attract foreign investment and create jobs.
"It will be difficult in Bulgaria until next spring. If we manage I expect afterwards steady revival and real development," Kostov told national radio in an interview.
On July 1, Bulgaria introduced a strict monetary regime known as a currency board, banning the central bank from lending to the government or commercial banks.
Kostov warned that the closure of loss-making state enterprises would increase unemployment in the months to come.
"The only remedy for this is the quickest possible attraction of foreign investment to Bulgaria and creation of investment activity among Bulgarian investors," he said.

Kostov said the government wanted to get big infrastructure projects under way such as the modernisation of Sofia airport, a gas pipeline to Turkey, and an oil pipeline to carry Russian crude from the Black Sea port of Bourgas to Alexandropolous in Greece.

He also cited a regional project for a main road from Albania via Macedonia to Bourgas and Varna on the Black Sea, and development of the Bulgarian Telecommunications Company after its forthcoming privatisation.
Kostov's centre-left government took office in May after early elections forced by month-long protests against the previous Socialist administration.

Previous Bulgarian governments since the end of communist rule failed to deliver on promises to sell off state enterprises and attract private sector finance to develop the country's dilapidated infrastructure.
The currency board system requires that the amount of levs in circulation be matched exactly by central bank foreign exchange reserves, pegging the lev at 1,000 to the mark.
Monthly inflation has steadily declined to 0.8 percent in June from 243 percent in February.
Last week, the International Monetary Fund praised the government's commitment to reform and its efforts to stabilise the economy but said there was no room for complacency.
It said discipline was needed on budget and economic policy, governance in the banking sector needed to be strengthened, and the government should improve the tax system.
